[_Comte_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")**Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec-Montfa**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Acte_naissance-1) (24 November 1864– 9 September 1901), known as **Toulouse-Lautrec** (French:[[tuluz lotʁɛk]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")), was a French painter, printmaker, draughtsman, caricaturist, and illustrator. His immersion in the colourful and theatrical life of [Paris's Belle Époque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_Belle_%C3%89poque "Paris in the Belle Époque") in the late 19th century allowed him to produce popular works of art from decadent affairs.

Born into the aristocracy, Toulouse-Lautrec broke both his legs during adolescence, leaving him with a stunted appearance. In later life, he developed an affinity for [brothels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brothel "Brothel") and prostitutes that directed the subject matter for many of his works, which record details of the late-19th-century bohemian lifestyle in Paris. He is among the painters described as [Post-Impressionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism "Post-Impressionism"), with [Paul Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne"), [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"), [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), and [Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat") also commonly considered as belonging in this loose group.

Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec-Montfa[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-2) was born at Demoiselles d'Imbert du Bosc (his great-aunts) home at rue de l'École Mage (presently 14, rue Henri de Toulouse Lautrec), Albi,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Acte_naissance-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-3) in the south of France, the firstborn child of [Count Alphonse de Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Alphonse_de_Toulouse-Lautrec_Montfa "Count Alphonse de Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa") (1838–1913)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-4) and Adèle Zoë Tapié de Celeyran (1841–1930).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-5) He was a member of an aristocratic family (descended from both the [Counts of Toulouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Toulouse "Count of Toulouse") and [Odet de Foix, Vicomte de Lautrec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odet_of_Foix,_Viscount_of_Lautrec "Odet of Foix, Viscount of Lautrec"), as well as the [Viscounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscount "Viscount") of [Montfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfa,_Tarn "Montfa, Tarn")). His younger brother was born in 1867 but died the following year.

Both sons enjoyed the [_titres de courtoisie_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtesy_title "Courtesy title") of _[Comte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-6) If Toulouse-Lautrec had outlived his father, he would have inherited the family [title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobility_of_France "Nobility of France") of _Comte de Toulouse-Lautrec_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-7)
After the death of his brother, Toulouse-Lautrec's parents separated, and a nanny cared for him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8) At the age of eight, Toulouse-Lautrec lived with his mother in Paris, where he drew sketches and caricatures in his exercise workbooks. A friend of his father, [René Princeteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Princeteau "René Princeteau"), sometimes visited to give informal lessons. Some of Toulouse-Lautrec's early paintings are of horses, a speciality of Princeteau's and a subject Toulouse-Lautrec later revisited in his "Circus Paintings".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-9)
In 1875, Toulouse-Lautrec returned to Albi because his mother had concerns about his health. He took thermal baths at [Amélie-les-Bains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am%C3%A9lie-les-Bains "Amélie-les-Bains"), and his mother consulted doctors in the hope of finding a way to improve her son's growth and development.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)

## Youth
**Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec Monfa** was born in Albi, Tarn in the Midi-Pyrenees region of France, the firstborn child of Comte Alphonse and Comtesse Adele de Toulouse-Lautrec. An aristocratic family (descendants of the Counts of Toulouse) that had recently fallen on hard times, the Toulouse-Lautrecs were feeling the effects of the inbreeding of past generations; the Comte and Comtesse themselves were first cousins, and Henri suffered from a number of congenital health conditions attributed to this tradition of inbreeding (see below). A younger brother was born to the family on 28 August 1867, but died the following year.
![Image 2: Self-Portrait. Caricature by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](https://www.toulouse-lautrec-foundation.org/api/img/henri-de-toulouse-lautrec/b/a/base_41026058.jpg?w=900&q=60&v=3)
Self-Portrait. Caricature · 1885

## Disability
At the age of 13 Henri fractured his left thigh bone, and at 14, the right. The breaks did not heal properly. Modern physicians attribute this to an unknown genetic disorder, possibly pycnodysostosis (also sometimes known as Toulouse-Lautrec Syndrome), or a variant disorder along the lines of osteopetrosis, achondroplasia, or osteogenesis imperfecta. Rickets aggravated with praecox virilism has also been suggested. His legs ceased to grow, so that as an adult he was only 1.54 m (5 ft 1 in) tall, having developed an adult-sized torso, while retaining his child-sized legs, which were 0.70 m (27.5 in) long. He is also reported to have had hypertrophied genitals.
Physically unable to participate in most of the activities typically enjoyed by men of his age, Toulouse-Lautrec immersed himself in his art. He became an important Post-Impressionist painter, art nouveau illustrator, and lithographer; and recorded in his works many details of the late-19th-century bohemian lifestyle in Paris. Toulouse-Lautrec also contributed a number of illustrations to the magazine Le Rire during the mid-1890s.
![Image 3: Party In Thr Moulin Rouge by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](https://www.toulouse-lautrec-foundation.org/api/img/henri-de-toulouse-lautrec/b/a/base_7126682.jpg?w=900&q=60&v=3)
Party In Thr Moulin Rouge

## Paris
Toulouse-Lautrec was drawn to Montmartre, an area of Paris famous for its bohemian lifestyle and for being the haunt of artists, writers, and philosophers. Tucked deep into Montmartre was the garden of Monsieur Pere Foret where Toulouse-Lautrec executed a series of pleasant plein-air paintings of Carmen Gaudin, the same red-head model who appears in The Laundress (1888). When the nearby Moulin Rouge cabaret opened its doors, Toulouse-Lautrec was commissioned to produce a series of posters. Thereafter, the cabaret reserved a seat for him, and displayed his paintings. Among the well-known works that he painted for the Moulin Rouge and other Parisian nightclubs are depictions of the singer Yvette Guilbert; the dancer Louise Weber, known as the outrageous La Goulue ("The Glutton"), who created the "French Can-Can"; and the much more subtle dancer Jane Avril.
Toulouse-Lautrec spent much time in brothels, where he was accepted by the prostitutes and madams to such an extent that he often moved in, and lived in a brothel for weeks at a time. He shared the lives of the women who made him their confidant, painting and drawing them at work and at leisure. Lautrec recorded their intimate relationships, which were often lesbian. A favourite model was a red-haired prostitute called Rosa la Rouge from whom he allegedly contracted syphilis.
Toulouse-Lautrec gave painting lessons to Suzanne Valadon, one of his models (and possibly his mistress as well).
An alcoholic for most of his adult life, Toulouse-Lautrec was placed in a sanatorium shortly before his death. He died from complications due to alcoholism and syphilis at the family estate in Malrome, fewer than three months before his 37th birthday. He is buried in Verdelais, Gironde, a few kilometers from the Chateau of Malrome, where he died.
Toulouse-Lautrec's last words reportedly were: "Le vieux con!" ("Old fool!")
**Tremblement de Terre**
The invention of the Tremblement de Terre is attributed to Toulouse-Lautrec, a potent mixture containing half absinthe and half cognac.

## Paris
![Image 4: Two Girls In Bed by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](https://www.toulouse-lautrec-foundation.org/api/img/henri-de-toulouse-lautrec/paintingsL/71319/two-girls-in-bed-reproduction-.jpg?w=900&q=60&v=3)
Two Girls In Bed

## Legacy
Throughout his career, which spanned less than 20 years, Toulouse-Lautrec created 737 canvases, 275 watercolors, 363 prints and posters, 5,084 drawings, some ceramic and stained glass work, and an unknown number of lost works. Toulouse-Lautrec is known along with Cezanne, Van Gogh, and Gaugin as one of the greatest painters of the Post-Impressionist period. His debt to the Impressionists, in particular the more figurative painters Manet and Degas, is apparent. In the works of Toulouse-Lautrec can be seen many parallels to Manet's bored barmaid at A Bar at the Folies-Bergere and the behind-the-scenes ballet dancers of Degas. He excelled at capturing people in their working environment, with the colour and the movement of the gaudy night-life present, but the glamour stripped away. He was masterly at capturing crowd scenes in which the figures are highly individualised. At the time that they were painted, the individual figures in his larger paintings could be identified by silhouette alone, and the names of many of these characters have been recorded. His treatment of his subject matter, whether as portraits, scenes of Parisian night-life, or intimate studies, has been described as both sympathetic and dispassionate.
Toulous-Lautrec's skilled depiction of people relied on his painterly style which is highly linear and gives great emphasis to contour. He often applied the paint in long, thin brushstrokes which often leave much of the board on which they are painted showing through. Many of his works may best be described as drawings in coloured paint.
After Toulouse-Lautrec's death, his mother, the Comtesse Adele Toulouse-Lautrec, and Maurice Joyant, his art dealer, promoted his art. His mother contributed funds for a museum to be built in Albi, his birthplace, to house his works. As of 2005, his paintings had sold for as much as US$14.5 million. (From Wikipedia)

As promised in a previous blog post([Michelangelo’s Sisters: (Re)Introducing Female Old Masters](https://artherstory.net/rediscovering-female-old-masters/)) here is a post that highlights the names and works of twelve female Old Masters. These dozen names represent only a small percentage of the women who were not only successful artists in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but were _famous_ for their art. Future posts will feature information about more women artists of the period, and samples of their work.

### Plautilla Nelli (1524**–**1588)
Born Pulisena Margherita Nelli, Suor Plautilla was a nun in Florence, and a follower of Savonarola. She taught herself to paint by copying other artists, notably Fra Bartolomeo. Her paintings—which include large-scale devotional works, wood lunettes, and miniatures—inspired the founding of [Advancing Women Artists](http://advancingwomenartists.org/home-1), AWA, which has ensured the restoration of some of her work. The restoration of Nelli’s 22-foot canvas depicting a Last Supper is due to be completed in 2019; see Jane Fortune’s 2017 [article](http://www.theflorentine.net/art-culture/2017/03/nelli-last-supper/) in _The Florentine_ about this painting. It is the only Last Supper known to be created by a Renaissance woman artist.
![Image 1](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Pained_Madonna.png)
_Pained Madonna_, 16th century, by Plautilla Nelli. The Museum of the Last Supper of Andrea del Sarto. Source: [Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pained_Madonna.png).
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/illuminating-women-artists-series-first-six-books/) about Catherine Turrill Lupi’s book on the artist, forthcoming from Lund Humphries.

### Catharina or Caterina van Hemessen (1528**–**after 1565)
Like many of early modernity’s women artists, Catharina van Hemessen was born into an artist family. Her father, Jan Sanders van Hemessen, was a prominent Mannerist painter in Antwerp. While she did paint a few religious-themed works, for the most part, Catharina van Hemessen was a portrait artist. She attracted the patronage of Maria of Austria; at Maria’s invitation, van Hemessen moved from the Netherlands to Spain. Upon Maria’s death, the painter was accorded a pension for life. The self-portrait shown here is the earliest known portrait of an artist (of either gender) at work at the easel.
![Image 2](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1920px-Hemessen-Selbstbildnis-1-781x1024.jpg)
_Self-Portrait at the Easel_, c. 1548, by Catharina van Hemessen. The Kunstmuseum Basel. Source: [Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hemessen-Selbstbildnis.jpg#/media/File:Hemessen-Selbstbildnis.jpg).

### Sofonisba Anguissola (1532**–**1625)
Born into an aristocratic family in Cremona, Italy, the oldest of seven children, Sofonisba Anguissola was an artistic prodigy. In her lifetime, her talent was noted by Michelangelo, Vasari, and Van Dyck. Unusually for a woman, she was permitted to apprentice as a painter. As a young woman, she spent some years in the court of Philip II as a lady-in-waiting (during which service she was able to continue painting). Her surviving works, which are held in museums all over the world, include at least sixteen self-portraits, from all stages of her life—from teenager to old woman. According to the [Museum of Fine Arts, Boston website](https://www.mfa.org/collections/object/self-portrait-33656), she “executed more self-portraits than any other artist in the period between Dürer and Rembrandt.”
![Image 3](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Sofonisba-Anguissola-Portr%C3%A6tgruppe-med-kunstnerens-fader-Amilcare-Anguissola-og-hendes-s%C3%B8skende-Minerva-og-Astrubale-ca.-1559.jpg)
_Portrait Group with the Artist’s Father Amilcare Anguissola and her Siblings Minerva and Astrubale_, c. 1559, by Sofonisba Anguissola. [Nivaagaards Malerisamling](http://www.nivaagaard.dk/en/artikel-en/renaissance/sofonisba-anguissola/). This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/sofonisba-anguissola/).

### Sofonisba Anguissola (1532**–**1625)
Read about Cecilia Gamberini’s book on the artist, co-published by [Lund Humphries](https://www.lundhumphries.com/products/sofonisba-anguissola) (UK/ROW) and [Getty Publications](https://shop.getty.edu/products/sofonisba-anguissola-978-1606069073?_pos=1&_psq=sofonisba&_ss=e&_v=1.0) (North America).

### Lavinia Fontana (1552**–**1614)
A Mannerist painter from Bologna, Italy, Fontana lays claim to a number of “firsts.” She is credited with being the first professional female artist. She was the first woman artist to paint female nudes, and possibly the first female to use live nude female models. She was the primary breadwinner for herself, her husband (also an artist) and their eleven children. She painted portraits, often of women, and also religious and mythological scenes. Fontana was elected into the Accademia di San Luca in Rome, where she and her family had moved at the invitation of Pope Clement VIII. She received numerous honors in her lifetime. As just one example, in 1611 sculptor and architect Felice Antonio Casoni cast a [bronze portrait medallion](https://www.nga.gov/collection/art-object-page.45169.html) of this artist! Read more about Fontana in Liz Lev’s [Art Herstory guest post](https://artherstory.net/lavinia-fontana-italys-first-female-professional-artist/).
![Image 4](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Lavinia-Fontana-Ginevra-Aldrovandi-Hercolani-The-Walters-842x1024.jpg)
_Portrait of Ginevra Aldrovandi Hercolani_, c. 1595,
by Lavinia Fontana. [The Walters Art Museum](https://art.thewalters.org/detail/13056/portrait-of-ginevra-aldrovandi-hercolani/). This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/lavinia-fontana-note-card/).
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/review-of-a-tale-of-two-women-painters/) about the 2019**–**20 Prado exhibition of works by Sofonisba Anguissola and Lavinia Fontana, “**‘**A Tale of Two Women Painters.”

### Artemisia Gentileschi (1593**–**after 1654)
Like her painter father Orazio Gentileschi, Artemisia Gentileschi was one of the Caravaggisti, followers of Caravaggio. She was born in Rome, where she was trained. Over the course of her career, she also worked in (at least) Florence, Naples, Venice and England. She attracted an international clientele, including members of the Medici house, and Charles I of England. Early in her career, she survived not only the trauma of abuse at the hands of a teacher, but also the trauma of the subsequent public trial. She specialized in painting women as allegory, and pictures of strong and suffering women from myths and the Bible.
![Image 5](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Artemisia-Gentileschi-front-Esther-before-Ahasuerus-The-Met-1024x756.jpg)
_Esther Before Ahasuerus_, 1628–1635, by Artemisia Gentileschi.
The [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436453). This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/gentileschi-esther/).
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/thoughts-on-by-her-hand-the-hartford-iteration/) about the exhibition “By Her Hand: Artemisia Gentileschi and Women Artists in Italy, 1500–1800,” which The Wadsworth Atheneum presented in Fall 2021. From February to May 2022, the show was hosted by the Detroit Institute of Arts.

### Artemisia Gentileschi (1593**–**after 1654)
Read about Sheila Barker’s book on the artist, co-published by [Lund Humphries](https://www.lundhumphries.com/products/artemisia-gentileschi?_pos=1&_sid=d94f9b148&_ss=r) (UK/ROW) and [Getty Publications](https://shop.getty.edu/products/artemisia-gentileschi-978-1606067338?_pos=1&_psq=artemisia+ge&_ss=e&_v=1.0) (North America).

### Giovanna Garzoni (1600**–**1670)
Today, Garzoni is best known for her delicate watercolor paintings of plants, vegetables, and animals. But she also painted religious, mythological, and allegorical subjects, as well as portraits. She is thought to have been born in Ascoli Piceno, Italy. If she married, the marriage was short-lived and ended in annulment. She is not known to have had children. She traveled and worked all over present-day Italy (including Venice, Naples, Rome, Turin and Florence) and in Paris. She left her estate to the Church of Santa Martina, the church of the Accademia di San Luca, in the understanding that she would be buried in that church.
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/giovanna-garzoni-uffizi-exhibition-review-june2020/) about the June 2020 Uffizi exhibition of Garzoni’s work, “‘The Greatness of the Universe’ in the art of Giovanna Garzoni.”
![Image 6](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2020/11/Giovanna-Garzoni-Still-Life-with-Citrons-the-J-Paul-Getty-Museum-front-1-1024x775.jpg)
_Still Life with Bowl of Citrons_,c. 1640s, by Giovanna Garzoni.[The J. Paul Getty Museum](https://www.getty.edu/art/collection/objects/131420/giovanna-garzoni-still-life-with-bowl-of-citrons-italian-late-1640s/). This image is reproduced on an[Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/giovanna-garzoni/).

### Judith Leyster (1609**–**1660)
Leyster, one of the first women to be admitted to the Saint Luke’s Guild of Haarlem, was a Dutch Golden Age painter of still lifes, portraits, and genre scenes. For almost 200 years after her death, experts attributed her works either to Frans Hals or to her husband, artist Jan Miense Molenaer. Many were re-attributed to her upon the discovery of her signature, a distinctive monogram of her initials which incorporates a shooting star—a play on words with her name, since Leyster means “lode star” in Dutch. Of her surviving works, she painted most in her young adulthood, before she married. But a self-portrait she painted later in life has recently come to light.
![Image 7](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Judith_Leyster_Boy_playing_the_Flute.jpg)
Judith Leyster Boy Playing the Flute
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/illuminating-women-artists-series-first-six-books/) about Frima Fox Hofrichter’s book on the artist, forthcoming from Lund Humphries.

### Louise Moillon (1610**–**1696)
Born into a family of artists—her father and her stepfather were painters and art dealers, and her brother was a painter—Louise Moillon specialized in still life painting, especially of fruits and vegetables. Her patrons included members of the French nobility, as well as Charles I of England. Most of the forty or so works attributed to her today are from before 1640, though a few are from the 1670s.
![Image 8](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/moillon.jpg)
_Still Life with a Basket of Fruit and a Bunch of Asparagus_, 1630, by Louise Moillon. The [Art Institute of Chicago.](https://www.artic.edu/artists/17526/louise-moillon) This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/louise-moillon/).
Read about Lesley Stevenson’s book on the artist, co-published by [Lund Humphries](https://www.lundhumphries.com/products/louise-moillon) (UK/ROW) and [Getty Publications](https://shop.getty.edu/products/louise-moillon-978-1606069028?_pos=1&_sid=0ecd5efcc&_ss=r) (North America).

### Mary Beale (c. 1633**–**1699)
Mary Beale, née Cradock, was one of the first professional female artists in England. She supported her family with her commissions and as an art teacher. Primarily a portrait artist, Beale painted many of the courtiers of Charles II. Her husband Charles acted as her business partner. His detailed notebooks provide a unique record of his wife’s daily activities, as well as of her business practices and expenses. Beale herself is author of _Observations_, an unpublished piece of instructional writing on painting.
![Image 9](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Beale.jpg)
_Mary Wither of Andwell_, early 1670s, by Mary Beale.
The [Art Gallery of South Australia](http://www.artgallery.sa.gov.au/agsa/home/Collection/detail.jsp?accNo=20038P59).
Read[here](https://www.lundhumphries.com/blogs/news-and-events/illuminating-women-artists-the-fifteen-volumes-under-contract-spring-2021)about Helen Draper’s book on the artist, forthcoming from Lund Humphries.

### Elisabetta Sirani (1638**–**1665)
By the time of her death at the age of only 27, Sirani was one of the most famous painters in Bologna. A former maid servant was tried, but acquitted, for having poisoning the artist. Historians now speculate that Sirani died of peritonitis, in the wake of a ruptured peptic ulcer. Her portraits, mythological subjects, and especially her images of the Holy Family and the Virgin and Child, gained her international fame. In addition to her artistic achievements, she founded an academy for women painters in Bologna. Read more about this artist in Adelina Modesti’s [Art Herstory guest post](https://artherstory.net/elisabetta-sirani/).
![Image 10](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Elisabetta-Sirani-Signora-Ortensia-Leoni-Cordini-as-Saint-Dorothy-Chazen-Art-Museum.jpg)
_Signora Ortensia Leoni Cordini as St. Dorothy_,1661, by Elisabetta Sirani. The [Chazen Museum of Art](http://embarkkiosk.chazen.wisc.edu/Obj12360?sid=13449&x=5098526).This image is reproduced on an[Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/elisabetta-sirani-note-card/).
Read about Adelina Modesti’s’s book on the artist, co-published by [Lund Humphries](https://www.lundhumphries.com/products/elisabetta-sirani) (UK/ROW) and [Getty Publications](https://shop.getty.edu/products/elisabetta-sirani-978-1606068175?_pos=1&_sid=3721ce391&_ss=r) (North America).

| [![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Toulouse-Lautrec-Monfa%2C_Henri_Marie_Raymond_de_1864-1901_13_Signature.jpg/250px-Toulouse-Lautrec-Monfa%2C_Henri_Marie_Raymond_de_1864-1901_13_Signature.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toulouse-Lautrec-Monfa,_Henri_Marie_Raymond_de_1864-1901_13_Signature.jpg) |
[_Comte_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")**Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec-Montfa**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Acte_naissance-1) (24 November 1864– 9 September 1901), known as **Toulouse-Lautrec** (French:[[tuluz lotʁɛk]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")), was a French painter, printmaker, draughtsman, caricaturist, and illustrator. His immersion in the colourful and theatrical life of [Paris's Belle Époque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_Belle_%C3%89poque "Paris in the Belle Époque") in the late 19th century allowed him to produce popular works of art from decadent affairs.
texts.2: Born into the aristocracy, Toulouse-Lautrec broke both his legs during adolescence, leaving him with a stunted appearance. In later life, he developed an affinity for [brothels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brothel "Brothel") and prostitutes that directed the subject matter for many of his works, which record details of the late-19th-century bohemian lifestyle in Paris. He is among the painters described as [Post-Impressionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism "Post-Impressionism"), with [Paul Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne"), [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"), [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), and [Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat") also commonly considered as belonging in this loose group.
texts.3: Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec-Montfa[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-2) was born at Demoiselles d'Imbert du Bosc (his great-aunts) home at rue de l'École Mage (presently 14, rue Henri de Toulouse Lautrec), Albi,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Acte_naissance-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-3) in the south of France, the firstborn child of [Count Alphonse de Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Alphonse_de_Toulouse-Lautrec_Montfa "Count Alphonse de Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa") (1838–1913)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-4) and Adèle Zoë Tapié de Celeyran (1841–1930).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-5) He was a member of an aristocratic family (descended from both the [Counts of Toulouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Toulouse "Count of Toulouse") and [Odet de Foix, Vicomte de Lautrec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odet_of_Foix,_Viscount_of_Lautrec "Odet of Foix, Viscount of Lautrec"), as well as the [Viscounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscount "Viscount") of [Montfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfa,_Tarn "Montfa, Tarn")). His younger brother was born in 1867 but died the following year.
texts.4:
Both sons enjoyed the [_titres de courtoisie_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtesy_title "Courtesy title") of _[Comte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-6) If Toulouse-Lautrec had outlived his father, he would have inherited the family [title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobility_of_France "Nobility of France") of _Comte de Toulouse-Lautrec_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-7)
After the death of his brother, Toulouse-Lautrec's parents separated, and a nanny cared for him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8) At the age of eight, Toulouse-Lautrec lived with his mother in Paris, where he drew sketches and caricatures in his exercise workbooks. A friend of his father, [René Princeteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Princeteau "René Princeteau"), sometimes visited to give informal lessons. Some of Toulouse-Lautrec's early paintings are of horses, a speciality of Princeteau's and a subject Toulouse-Lautrec later revisited in his "Circus Paintings".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-9)
In 1875, Toulouse-Lautrec returned to Albi because his mother had concerns about his health. He took thermal baths at [Amélie-les-Bains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am%C3%A9lie-les-Bains "Amélie-les-Bains"), and his mother consulted doctors in the hope of finding a way to improve her son's growth and development.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)

### Disability and health problems
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Disability and health problems")]
[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Guibert_2.jpg/250px-Guibert_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guibert_2.jpg)
Mr. Toulouse paints Mr. Lautrec (c.1891), a photomontage by [Maurice Guibert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Guibert "Maurice Guibert")
Toulouse-Lautrec's parents were [first cousins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_cousins "First cousins") (their mothers were sisters),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-10) and his [congenital health conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congenital_disorder "Congenital disorder") have often been attributed to a family history of [inbreeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbreeding "Inbreeding").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-11)
texts.6:
### Disability and health problems
At the age of 13, Toulouse-Lautrec fractured his right [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur"), and at age 14, he fractured his left femur.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TheTimes-12) The breaks did not heal properly. Modern physicians attribute this to an unknown [genetic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_disorder "Genetic disorder"), possibly [pycnodysostosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pycnodysostosis "Pycnodysostosis") (sometimes known as 'Toulouse-Lautrec Syndrome'),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Valdes-Socin_2021-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Angier-14) or a variant disorder along the lines of [osteopetrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteopetrosis "Osteopetrosis"), [achondroplasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achondroplasia "Achondroplasia"), or [osteogenesis imperfecta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteogenesis_imperfecta "Osteogenesis imperfecta").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-15) Toulouse-Lautrec's legs ceased to grow when he reached 1.52 m (5 ft 0 in).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-16) He developed an adult torso while retaining his child-sized legs.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-17)

texts.8:
### Disability and health problems
During a stay in [Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice,_France "Nice, France") on the [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera"), his progress in painting and drawing impressed Princeteau, who persuaded Toulouse-Lautrec's parents to allow him to return to Paris and study under the portrait painter [Léon Bonnat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Bonnat "Léon Bonnat"). He returned to Paris in 1882.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-19) Toulouse-Lautrec's mother had high ambitions and, with the aim of her son becoming a fashionable and respected painter, used their family's influence to gain him entry to Bonnat's studio.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8) He was drawn to [Montmartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montmartre "Montmartre"), the area of Paris known for its bohemian lifestyle and the haunt of artists, writers, and philosophers. Studying with Bonnat placed Toulouse-Lautrec in the heart of Montmartre, an area he rarely left over the next 20 years.
texts.9:
### Disability and health problems
After Bonnat took a new job, Toulouse-Lautrec moved to the studio of [Fernand Cormon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernand_Cormon "Fernand Cormon") in 1882 and studied for a further five years and established the group of friends he kept for the rest of his life. At this time, he met [Émile Bernard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Bernard_(painter) "Émile Bernard (painter)") and [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"). Cormon, whose instruction was more relaxed than Bonnat's, allowed his pupils to roam Paris, looking for subjects to paint. During this period, Toulouse-Lautrec had his first encounter with a prostitute (reputedly sponsored by his friends), which led him to paint his first painting of a prostitute in [Montmartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montmartre "Montmartre"), a woman rumoured to be Marie-Charlet.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)
[![Image 5: A thin woman's back and hair are prominent. | [![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Toulouse-Lautrec-Monfa%2C_Henri_Marie_Raymond_de_1864-1901_13_Signature.jpg/250px-Toulouse-Lautrec-Monfa%2C_Henri_Marie_Raymond_de_1864-1901_13_Signature.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Toulouse-Lautrec-Monfa,_Henri_Marie_Raymond_de_1864-1901_13_Signature.jpg) |
[_Comte_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")**Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec-Montfa**[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Acte_naissance-1) (24 November 1864– 9 September 1901), known as **Toulouse-Lautrec** (French:[[tuluz lotʁɛk]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")), was a French painter, printmaker, draughtsman, caricaturist, and illustrator. His immersion in the colourful and theatrical life of [Paris's Belle Époque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_in_the_Belle_%C3%89poque "Paris in the Belle Époque") in the late 19th century allowed him to produce popular works of art from decadent affairs.
texts.2: Born into the aristocracy, Toulouse-Lautrec broke both his legs during adolescence, leaving him with a stunted appearance. In later life, he developed an affinity for [brothels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brothel "Brothel") and prostitutes that directed the subject matter for many of his works, which record details of the late-19th-century bohemian lifestyle in Paris. He is among the painters described as [Post-Impressionists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-Impressionism "Post-Impressionism"), with [Paul Cézanne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_C%C3%A9zanne "Paul Cézanne"), [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"), [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), and [Georges Seurat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Seurat "Georges Seurat") also commonly considered as belonging in this loose group.
texts.3: Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec-Montfa[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-2) was born at Demoiselles d'Imbert du Bosc (his great-aunts) home at rue de l'École Mage (presently 14, rue Henri de Toulouse Lautrec), Albi,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Acte_naissance-1)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-3) in the south of France, the firstborn child of [Count Alphonse de Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_Alphonse_de_Toulouse-Lautrec_Montfa "Count Alphonse de Toulouse-Lautrec Montfa") (1838–1913)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-4) and Adèle Zoë Tapié de Celeyran (1841–1930).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-5) He was a member of an aristocratic family (descended from both the [Counts of Toulouse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Toulouse "Count of Toulouse") and [Odet de Foix, Vicomte de Lautrec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odet_of_Foix,_Viscount_of_Lautrec "Odet of Foix, Viscount of Lautrec"), as well as the [Viscounts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viscount "Viscount") of [Montfa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montfa,_Tarn "Montfa, Tarn")). His younger brother was born in 1867 but died the following year.
texts.4:
Both sons enjoyed the [_titres de courtoisie_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Courtesy_title "Courtesy title") of _[Comte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count "Count")_.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-6) If Toulouse-Lautrec had outlived his father, he would have inherited the family [title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobility_of_France "Nobility of France") of _Comte de Toulouse-Lautrec_.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-7)
After the death of his brother, Toulouse-Lautrec's parents separated, and a nanny cared for him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8) At the age of eight, Toulouse-Lautrec lived with his mother in Paris, where he drew sketches and caricatures in his exercise workbooks. A friend of his father, [René Princeteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Princeteau "René Princeteau"), sometimes visited to give informal lessons. Some of Toulouse-Lautrec's early paintings are of horses, a speciality of Princeteau's and a subject Toulouse-Lautrec later revisited in his "Circus Paintings".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-9)
In 1875, Toulouse-Lautrec returned to Albi because his mother had concerns about his health. He took thermal baths at [Amélie-les-Bains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Am%C3%A9lie-les-Bains "Amélie-les-Bains"), and his mother consulted doctors in the hope of finding a way to improve her son's growth and development.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)

### Disability and health problems
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Henri_de_Toulouse-Lautrec&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Disability and health problems")]
[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/95/Guibert_2.jpg/250px-Guibert_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Guibert_2.jpg)
Mr. Toulouse paints Mr. Lautrec (c.1891), a photomontage by [Maurice Guibert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Guibert "Maurice Guibert")
Toulouse-Lautrec's parents were [first cousins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_cousins "First cousins") (their mothers were sisters),[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-10) and his [congenital health conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congenital_disorder "Congenital disorder") have often been attributed to a family history of [inbreeding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inbreeding "Inbreeding").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-11)
texts.6:
### Disability and health problems
At the age of 13, Toulouse-Lautrec fractured his right [femur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Femur "Femur"), and at age 14, he fractured his left femur.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TheTimes-12) The breaks did not heal properly. Modern physicians attribute this to an unknown [genetic disorder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_disorder "Genetic disorder"), possibly [pycnodysostosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pycnodysostosis "Pycnodysostosis") (sometimes known as 'Toulouse-Lautrec Syndrome'),[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Valdes-Socin_2021-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-Angier-14) or a variant disorder along the lines of [osteopetrosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteopetrosis "Osteopetrosis"), [achondroplasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achondroplasia "Achondroplasia"), or [osteogenesis imperfecta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osteogenesis_imperfecta "Osteogenesis imperfecta").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-15) Toulouse-Lautrec's legs ceased to grow when he reached 1.52 m (5 ft 0 in).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-16) He developed an adult torso while retaining his child-sized legs.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-17)

### Disability and health problems
During a stay in [Nice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nice,_France "Nice, France") on the [French Riviera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Riviera "French Riviera"), his progress in painting and drawing impressed Princeteau, who persuaded Toulouse-Lautrec's parents to allow him to return to Paris and study under the portrait painter [Léon Bonnat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on_Bonnat "Léon Bonnat"). He returned to Paris in 1882.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-19) Toulouse-Lautrec's mother had high ambitions and, with the aim of her son becoming a fashionable and respected painter, used their family's influence to gain him entry to Bonnat's studio.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8) He was drawn to [Montmartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montmartre "Montmartre"), the area of Paris known for its bohemian lifestyle and the haunt of artists, writers, and philosophers. Studying with Bonnat placed Toulouse-Lautrec in the heart of Montmartre, an area he rarely left over the next 20 years.
texts.9:
### Disability and health problems
After Bonnat took a new job, Toulouse-Lautrec moved to the studio of [Fernand Cormon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernand_Cormon "Fernand Cormon") in 1882 and studied for a further five years and established the group of friends he kept for the rest of his life. At this time, he met [Émile Bernard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89mile_Bernard_(painter) "Émile Bernard (painter)") and [Vincent van Gogh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_van_Gogh "Vincent van Gogh"). Cormon, whose instruction was more relaxed than Bonnat's, allowed his pupils to roam Paris, looking for subjects to paint. During this period, Toulouse-Lautrec had his first encounter with a prostitute (reputedly sponsored by his friends), which led him to paint his first painting of a prostitute in [Montmartre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montmartre "Montmartre"), a woman rumoured to be Marie-Charlet.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toulouse-Lautrec#cite_note-TL-Book1-8)

texts.0: As promised in a previous blog post([Michelangelo’s Sisters: (Re)Introducing Female Old Masters](https://artherstory.net/rediscovering-female-old-masters/)) here is a post that highlights the names and works of twelve female Old Masters. These dozen names represent only a small percentage of the women who were not only successful artists in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but were _famous_ for their art. Future posts will feature information about more women artists of the period, and samples of their work.
texts.1:
### Plautilla Nelli (1524**–**1588)
Born Pulisena Margherita Nelli, Suor Plautilla was a nun in Florence, and a follower of Savonarola. She taught herself to paint by copying other artists, notably Fra Bartolomeo. Her paintings—which include large-scale devotional works, wood lunettes, and miniatures—inspired the founding of [Advancing Women Artists](http://advancingwomenartists.org/home-1), AWA, which has ensured the restoration of some of her work. The restoration of Nelli’s 22-foot canvas depicting a Last Supper is due to be completed in 2019; see Jane Fortune’s 2017 [article](http://www.theflorentine.net/art-culture/2017/03/nelli-last-supper/) in _The Florentine_ about this painting. It is the only Last Supper known to be created by a Renaissance woman artist.
![Image 1](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Pained_Madonna.png)
_Pained Madonna_, 16th century, by Plautilla Nelli. The Museum of the Last Supper of Andrea del Sarto. Source: [Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Pained_Madonna.png).
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/illuminating-women-artists-series-first-six-books/) about Catherine Turrill Lupi’s book on the artist, forthcoming from Lund Humphries.
texts.2:
### Catharina or Caterina van Hemessen (1528**–**after 1565)
Like many of early modernity’s women artists, Catharina van Hemessen was born into an artist family. Her father, Jan Sanders van Hemessen, was a prominent Mannerist painter in Antwerp. While she did paint a few religious-themed works, for the most part, Catharina van Hemessen was a portrait artist. She attracted the patronage of Maria of Austria; at Maria’s invitation, van Hemessen moved from the Netherlands to Spain. Upon Maria’s death, the painter was accorded a pension for life. The self-portrait shown here is the earliest known portrait of an artist (of either gender) at work at the easel.
![Image 2](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/1920px-Hemessen-Selbstbildnis-1-781x1024.jpg)
_Self-Portrait at the Easel_, c. 1548, by Catharina van Hemessen. The Kunstmuseum Basel. Source: [Wikimedia](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hemessen-Selbstbildnis.jpg#/media/File:Hemessen-Selbstbildnis.jpg).
texts.3:
### Sofonisba Anguissola (1532**–**1625)
Born into an aristocratic family in Cremona, Italy, the oldest of seven children, Sofonisba Anguissola was an artistic prodigy. In her lifetime, her talent was noted by Michelangelo, Vasari, and Van Dyck. Unusually for a woman, she was permitted to apprentice as a painter. As a young woman, she spent some years in the court of Philip II as a lady-in-waiting (during which service she was able to continue painting). Her surviving works, which are held in museums all over the world, include at least sixteen self-portraits, from all stages of her life—from teenager to old woman. According to the [Museum of Fine Arts, Boston website](https://www.mfa.org/collections/object/self-portrait-33656), she “executed more self-portraits than any other artist in the period between Dürer and Rembrandt.”
![Image 3](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Sofonisba-Anguissola-Portr%C3%A6tgruppe-med-kunstnerens-fader-Amilcare-Anguissola-og-hendes-s%C3%B8skende-Minerva-og-Astrubale-ca.-1559.jpg)
_Portrait Group with the Artist’s Father Amilcare Anguissola and her Siblings Minerva and Astrubale_, c. 1559, by Sofonisba Anguissola. [Nivaagaards Malerisamling](http://www.nivaagaard.dk/en/artikel-en/renaissance/sofonisba-anguissola/). This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/sofonisba-anguissola/).

### Lavinia Fontana (1552**–**1614)
A Mannerist painter from Bologna, Italy, Fontana lays claim to a number of “firsts.” She is credited with being the first professional female artist. She was the first woman artist to paint female nudes, and possibly the first female to use live nude female models. She was the primary breadwinner for herself, her husband (also an artist) and their eleven children. She painted portraits, often of women, and also religious and mythological scenes. Fontana was elected into the Accademia di San Luca in Rome, where she and her family had moved at the invitation of Pope Clement VIII. She received numerous honors in her lifetime. As just one example, in 1611 sculptor and architect Felice Antonio Casoni cast a [bronze portrait medallion](https://www.nga.gov/collection/art-object-page.45169.html) of this artist! Read more about Fontana in Liz Lev’s [Art Herstory guest post](https://artherstory.net/lavinia-fontana-italys-first-female-professional-artist/).
![Image 4](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/03/Lavinia-Fontana-Ginevra-Aldrovandi-Hercolani-The-Walters-842x1024.jpg)
_Portrait of Ginevra Aldrovandi Hercolani_, c. 1595,
by Lavinia Fontana. [The Walters Art Museum](https://art.thewalters.org/detail/13056/portrait-of-ginevra-aldrovandi-hercolani/). This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/lavinia-fontana-note-card/).
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/review-of-a-tale-of-two-women-painters/) about the 2019**–**20 Prado exhibition of works by Sofonisba Anguissola and Lavinia Fontana, “**‘**A Tale of Two Women Painters.”

### Artemisia Gentileschi (1593**–**after 1654)
Like her painter father Orazio Gentileschi, Artemisia Gentileschi was one of the Caravaggisti, followers of Caravaggio. She was born in Rome, where she was trained. Over the course of her career, she also worked in (at least) Florence, Naples, Venice and England. She attracted an international clientele, including members of the Medici house, and Charles I of England. Early in her career, she survived not only the trauma of abuse at the hands of a teacher, but also the trauma of the subsequent public trial. She specialized in painting women as allegory, and pictures of strong and suffering women from myths and the Bible.
![Image 5](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Artemisia-Gentileschi-front-Esther-before-Ahasuerus-The-Met-1024x756.jpg)
_Esther Before Ahasuerus_, 1628–1635, by Artemisia Gentileschi.
The [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/436453). This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/gentileschi-esther/).
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/thoughts-on-by-her-hand-the-hartford-iteration/) about the exhibition “By Her Hand: Artemisia Gentileschi and Women Artists in Italy, 1500–1800,” which The Wadsworth Atheneum presented in Fall 2021. From February to May 2022, the show was hosted by the Detroit Institute of Arts.

### Giovanna Garzoni (1600**–**1670)
Today, Garzoni is best known for her delicate watercolor paintings of plants, vegetables, and animals. But she also painted religious, mythological, and allegorical subjects, as well as portraits. She is thought to have been born in Ascoli Piceno, Italy. If she married, the marriage was short-lived and ended in annulment. She is not known to have had children. She traveled and worked all over present-day Italy (including Venice, Naples, Rome, Turin and Florence) and in Paris. She left her estate to the Church of Santa Martina, the church of the Accademia di San Luca, in the understanding that she would be buried in that church.
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/giovanna-garzoni-uffizi-exhibition-review-june2020/) about the June 2020 Uffizi exhibition of Garzoni’s work, “‘The Greatness of the Universe’ in the art of Giovanna Garzoni.”

_Still Life with Bowl of Citrons_,c. 1640s, by Giovanna Garzoni.[The J. Paul Getty Museum](https://www.getty.edu/art/collection/objects/131420/giovanna-garzoni-still-life-with-bowl-of-citrons-italian-late-1640s/). ### Judith Leyster (1609**–**1660)
Leyster, one of the first women to be admitted to the Saint Luke’s Guild of Haarlem, was a Dutch Golden Age painter of still lifes, portraits, and genre scenes. For almost 200 years after her death, experts attributed her works either to Frans Hals or to her husband, artist Jan Miense Molenaer. Many were re-attributed to her upon the discovery of her signature, a distinctive monogram of her initials which incorporates a shooting star—a play on words with her name, since Leyster means “lode star” in Dutch. Of her surviving works, she painted most in her young adulthood, before she married. But a self-portrait she painted later in life has recently come to light.
![Image 7](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/01/Judith_Leyster_Boy_playing_the_Flute.jpg)
Judith Leyster Boy Playing the Flute
Read [here](https://artherstory.net/illuminating-women-artists-series-first-six-books/) about Frima Fox Hofrichter’s book on the artist, forthcoming from Lund Humphries.
texts.10:
### Louise Moillon (1610**–**1696)
Born into a family of artists—her father and her stepfather were painters and art dealers, and her brother was a painter—Louise Moillon specialized in still life painting, especially of fruits and vegetables. Her patrons included members of the French nobility, as well as Charles I of England. Most of the forty or so works attributed to her today are from before 1640, though a few are from the 1670s.
![Image 8](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/moillon.jpg)
_Still Life with a Basket of Fruit and a Bunch of Asparagus_, 1630, by Louise Moillon. The [Art Institute of Chicago.](https://www.artic.edu/artists/17526/louise-moillon) This image is reproduced on an [Art Herstory note card](https://artherstory.net/product/louise-moillon/).
Read about Lesley Stevenson’s book on the artist, co-published by [Lund Humphries](https://www.lundhumphries.com/products/louise-moillon) (UK/ROW) and [Getty Publications](https://shop.getty.edu/products/louise-moillon-978-1606069028?_pos=1&_sid=0ecd5efcc&_ss=r) (North America).
texts.11:
### Mary Beale (c. 1633**–**1699)
Mary Beale, née Cradock, was one of the first professional female artists in England. She supported her family with her commissions and as an art teacher. Primarily a portrait artist, Beale painted many of the courtiers of Charles II. Her husband Charles acted as her business partner. His detailed notebooks provide a unique record of his wife’s daily activities, as well as of her business practices and expenses. Beale herself is author of _Observations_, an unpublished piece of instructional writing on painting.
![Image 9](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/Beale.jpg)
_Mary Wither of Andwell_, early 1670s, by Mary Beale.
The [Art Gallery of South Australia](http://www.artgallery.sa.gov.au/agsa/home/Collection/detail.jsp?accNo=20038P59).
Read[here](https://www.lundhumphries.com/blogs/news-and-events/illuminating-women-artists-the-fifteen-volumes-under-contract-spring-2021)about Helen Draper’s book on the artist, forthcoming from Lund Humphries.
texts.12:
### Elisabetta Sirani (1638**–**1665)
By the time of her death at the age of only 27, Sirani was one of the most famous painters in Bologna. A former maid servant was tried, but acquitted, for having poisoning the artist. Historians now speculate that Sirani died of peritonitis, in the wake of a ruptured peptic ulcer. Her portraits, mythological subjects, and especially her images of the Holy Family and the Virgin and Child, gained her international fame. In addition to her artistic achievements, she founded an academy for women painters in Bologna. Read more about this artist in Adelina Modesti’s [Art Herstory guest post](https://artherstory.net/elisabetta-sirani/).
![Image 10](https://artherstory.net/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Elisabetta-Sirani-Signora-Ortensia-Leoni-Cordini-as-Saint-Dorothy-Chazen-Art-Museum.jpg)

texts.1:
## Youth
**Henri Marie Raymond de Toulouse-Lautrec Monfa** was born in Albi, Tarn in the Midi-Pyrenees region of France, the firstborn child of Comte Alphonse and Comtesse Adele de Toulouse-Lautrec. An aristocratic family (descendants of the Counts of Toulouse) that had recently fallen on hard times, the Toulouse-Lautrecs were feeling the effects of the inbreeding of past generations; the Comte and Comtesse themselves were first cousins, and Henri suffered from a number of congenital health conditions attributed to this tradition of inbreeding (see below). A younger brother was born to the family on 28 August 1867, but died the following year.
![Image 2: Self-Portrait. Caricature by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](https://www.toulouse-lautrec-foundation.org/api/img/henri-de-toulouse-lautrec/b/a/base_41026058.jpg?w=900&q=60&v=3)
Self-Portrait. Caricature · 1885
texts.2:
## Disability
At the age of 13 Henri fractured his left thigh bone, and at 14, the right. The breaks did not heal properly. Modern physicians attribute this to an unknown genetic disorder, possibly pycnodysostosis (also sometimes known as Toulouse-Lautrec Syndrome), or a variant disorder along the lines of osteopetrosis, achondroplasia, or osteogenesis imperfecta. Rickets aggravated with praecox virilism has also been suggested. His legs ceased to grow, so that as an adult he was only 1.54 m (5 ft 1 in) tall, having developed an adult-sized torso, while retaining his child-sized legs, which were 0.70 m (27.5 in) long. He is also reported to have had hypertrophied genitals.
Physically unable to participate in most of the activities typically enjoyed by men of his age, Toulouse-Lautrec immersed himself in his art. He became an important Post-Impressionist painter, art nouveau illustrator, and lithographer; and recorded in his works many details of the late-19th-century bohemian lifestyle in Paris. Toulouse-Lautrec also contributed a number of illustrations to the magazine Le Rire during the mid-1890s.
![Image 3: Party In Thr Moulin Rouge by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](https://www.toulouse-lautrec-foundation.org/api/img/henri-de-toulouse-lautrec/b/a/base_7126682.jpg?w=900&q=60&v=3)
Party In Thr Moulin Rouge
texts.3:
## Paris
Toulouse-Lautrec was drawn to Montmartre, an area of Paris famous for its bohemian lifestyle and for being the haunt of artists, writers, and philosophers. Tucked deep into Montmartre was the garden of Monsieur Pere Foret where Toulouse-Lautrec executed a series of pleasant plein-air paintings of Carmen Gaudin, the same red-head model who appears in The Laundress (1888). When the nearby Moulin Rouge cabaret opened its doors, Toulouse-Lautrec was commissioned to produce a series of posters. Thereafter, the cabaret reserved a seat for him, and displayed his paintings. Among the well-known works that he painted for the Moulin Rouge and other Parisian nightclubs are depictions of the singer Yvette Guilbert; the dancer Louise Weber, known as the outrageous La Goulue ("The Glutton"), who created the "French Can-Can"; and the much more subtle dancer Jane Avril.
Toulouse-Lautrec spent much time in brothels, where he was accepted by the prostitutes and madams to such an extent that he often moved in, and lived in a brothel for weeks at a time. He shared the lives of the women who made him their confidant, painting and drawing them at work and at leisure. Lautrec recorded their intimate relationships, which were often lesbian. A favourite model was a red-haired prostitute called Rosa la Rouge from whom he allegedly contracted syphilis.
Toulouse-Lautrec gave painting lessons to Suzanne Valadon, one of his models (and possibly his mistress as well).
An alcoholic for most of his adult life, Toulouse-Lautrec was placed in a sanatorium shortly before his death. He died from complications due to alcoholism and syphilis at the family estate in Malrome, fewer than three months before his 37th birthday. He is buried in Verdelais, Gironde, a few kilometers from the Chateau of Malrome, where he died.
Toulouse-Lautrec's last words reportedly were: "Le vieux con!" ("Old fool!")
**Tremblement de Terre**
The invention of the Tremblement de Terre is attributed to Toulouse-Lautrec, a potent mixture containing half absinthe and half cognac.
texts.4:
## Paris
![Image 4: Two Girls In Bed by Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec](https://www.toulouse-lautrec-foundation.org/api/img/henri-de-toulouse-lautrec/paintingsL/71319/two-girls-in-bed-reproduction-.jpg?w=900&q=60&v=3)
Two Girls In Bed
texts.5:
## Legacy
Throughout his career, which spanned less than 20 years, Toulouse-Lautrec created 737 canvases, 275 watercolors, 363 prints and posters, 5,084 drawings, some ceramic and stained glass work, and an unknown number of lost works. Toulouse-Lautrec is known along with Cezanne, Van Gogh, and Gaugin as one of the greatest painters of the Post-Impressionist period. His debt to the Impressionists, in particular the more figurative painters Manet and Degas, is apparent. In the works of Toulouse-Lautrec can be seen many parallels to Manet's bored barmaid at A Bar at the Folies-Bergere and the behind-the-scenes ballet dancers of Degas. He excelled at capturing people in their working environment, with the colour and the movement of the gaudy night-life present, but the glamour stripped away. He was masterly at capturing crowd scenes in which the figures are highly individualised. At the time that they were painted, the individual figures in his larger paintings could be identified by silhouette alone, and the names of many of these characters have been recorded. His treatment of his subject matter, whether as portraits, scenes of Parisian night-life, or intimate studies, has been described as both sympathetic and dispassionate.
Toulous-Lautrec's skilled depiction of people relied on his painterly style which is highly linear and gives great emphasis to contour. He often applied the paint in long, thin brushstrokes which often leave much of the board on which they are painted showing through. Many of his works may best be described as drawings in coloured paint.
After Toulouse-Lautrec's death, his mother, the Comtesse Adele Toulouse-Lautrec, and Maurice Joyant, his art dealer, promoted his art. His mother contributed funds for a museum to be built in Albi, his birthplace, to house his works. As of 2005, his paintings had sold for as much as US$14.5 million. (From Wikipedia)

opened.information:
Source: https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/articleshowprint/126410420.cms
Title: After consecutive terms from 2014, 102 MPs’ assets up 110%: Report - Times of India
Chunks: 0,1
NEW DELHI : An analysis of assets of 102 members of Lok Sabha who got elected for three consecutive terms from 2014 to 2024 shows that they recorded average percentage growth of 110%.The report by Association for Democratic Reforms (ADR) and National Election Watch shows that the average value of assets of these 102 re-elected MPs fielded by various parties was Rs 15.76 crore in 2014, Rs 24.21 crore in 2019 and Rs 33.13 crore in 2024.
Winter Session Closes As Lok Sabha Skips Pollution Debate A Day After G RAM G Bill Sparks Chaos
05:26
![Image 1: Winter Session Closes As Lok Sabha Skips Pollution Debate A Day After G RAM G Bill Sparks Chaos](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/42706777.gif)
![Image 2: Loading](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/photo/42715392.cms)
The average asset growth for these 102 MPs between the 2014 and 2024 Lok Sabha elections is Rs 17.36 crore.
The report is based on analysis of the self-sworn affidavits of 102 out of 103 reelected MPs in the 2014-2024 period. “Due to the nonavailability of 2019 Lok Sabha affidavit data, Devendra Singh, alias Bhole Singh, BJP MP from Akbarpur, UP, has not been included in this analysis,” the report states.
The report also lists the 10 re-elected MPs who saw the highest increase in their assets (rupee-wise). Topping this list is Shrimant Chh Udayanraje Pratapsinhamaharaj Bhonsle of BJP from Satara seat, whose assets increased by Rs 162.51 crore, from Rs 60.60 crore in 2014 to Rs 223.12 crore in 2024.

The assets of Poonamben Hematbhai Maadam of BJP from Gujarat’s Jamnagar constituency increased by Rs 130.26 crore, from Rs 17.43 crore in 2014 to Rs 147.70 crore in 2024.
The assets of P V Midhun Reddy of YSRCP from Andhra’s Rajampet constituency rose by Rs 124.25 crore, from Rs 22.59 crore in 2014 to Rs 146.85 crore in 2024.
In terms of the highest percentage increase, the assets of Shiv Sena MP from Kalyan, Shrikant Eknath Shinde, increased from Rs 9.98 lakh in 2014 to Rs 14.92 crore in 2024, recording growth of 14,851%. On the other hand, the assets of only 1 MP, CR Patil from BJP, who represents Navsari in Gujarat, declined from Rs 74.47 crore in 2014 to Rs 39.49 crore in 2024.
The assets of PM Narendra Modi, MP from Varanasi, rose by 82% from Rs 1.65 crore in 2014 to Rs 3.02 crore in 2024. The assets of leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi rose by 117% from Rs 9.40 crore in 2014 to Rs 20.39 crore in 2024.

# Ujjain Lok Sabha Election results 2024
Ujjain, a Lok Sabha constituency in Madhya Pradesh, was formed in 1951 and is one of 29 constituencies in the state. It includes Ujjain and part of Ratlam district. Reserved for scheduled caste candidates since 1966, the 2019 election saw Anil Firojiya of BJP emerge victorious with a significant margin of 3,65,637 votes over Babulal Malviya of INC. Firojiya secured 7,91,663 votes, retaining his position as the current MP. The constituency comprises Mahidpur, Ujjain Dakshin, Nagada-khachrod, Tarana (sc), Alot (sc), Badnagar, Ujjain Uttar, and Ghatiya (sc) assembly constituencies. Notable for a 75.33% voter turnout in 2019, 10 candidates contested. Ujjain Lok Sabha constituency remains a significant political area in Madhya Pradesh.

# Ujjain Lok Sabha Election results 2024
Ujjain, a Lok Sabha constituency in Madhya Pradesh, was formed in 1951 and is one of 29 constituencies in the state. It includes Ujjain and part of Ratlam district. Reserved for scheduled caste candidates since 1966, the 2019 election saw Anil Firojiya of BJP emerge victorious with a significant margin of 3,65,637 votes over Babulal Malviya of INC. Firojiya secured 7,91,663 votes, retaining his position as the current MP. The constituency comprises Mahidpur, Ujjain Dakshin, Nagada-khachrod, Tarana (sc), Alot (sc), Badnagar, Ujjain Uttar, and Ghatiya (sc) assembly constituencies. Notable for a 75.33% voter turnout in 2019, 10 candidates contested. Ujjain Lok Sabha constituency remains a significant political area in Madhya Pradesh.
